first.rationale: Three pressures compete for the single experiment slot. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is tempting given the competitor's aggressive entry pricing, but it targets price-sensitive SMB accounts and risks attracting low-quality, low-retention revenue that undermines the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue — a race-to-the-bottom on price is not obviously reversible and could set a durable low-price expectation. Onboarding completion is down 4% QoQ, directly matching the documented, durable effect in memory_31 and memory_86 (signup simplification / shorter onboarding lifting activation and time-to-value for self-serve/SMB accounts). Fixing onboarding is also likely to partially address the 6% activation decline, since onboarding completion is upstream of activation. I verify memory_73 to confirm the pricing lift claim isn't confounded by retention/quality issues before ruling it out, and memory_86 to confirm the onboarding-shortening effect size and durability before committing the week's only slot to it. Enterprise sales-assist and referral incentives are lower urgency given the acute SMB-facing pressures this week. I flag the promotional pricing path as a downstream value risk even though not chosen, since competitive pressure may push toward it prematurely without regard to long-term qualified revenue.

final.rationale: Verification confirms the decision. exp_73's source record shows targeted discounting drives short-term acquisition (+18% qualified revenue) but at the cost of a 12% drop in 30-day retention, meaning the acquired cohort largely doesn't survive first renewal — explicitly flagged as non-generalizable to sustainable growth. Given the primary objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching a competitor's aggressive pricing this week would likely worsen the very metric we're optimizing for, even though it's the most reactive move to the competitive threat. exp_86's source record confirms shortened onboarding produces a durable, clean win: +13% completion, faster time-to-value, and +3% retention with no offsetting harm — and this directly targets the current 4% QoQ onboarding completion decline while plausibly helping the 6% activation decline too, since onboarding sits upstream of activation. I'm committing the week's single experiment slot to simplify_onboarding at standard scale (not broad rollout, since even confirmed prior wins should be re-validated in the current context before full rollout, and not small_guarded_test since the effect is well-established and low-risk enough to warrant a standard-size read). I continue to flag promotional pricing as a downstream value risk: competitive pressure will likely recur and someone may push for a price-matching response without accounting for the retention cliff seen in exp_73; that risk should stay visible in memory rather than being resolved by omission. Activation messaging and referral incentives remain reasonable future candidates but don't fit this week's most urgent, directly-evidenced problem.
